utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Good afternoon to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning -- good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio; Ms. Joanne Richardson; and our case manager Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And also good afternoon to the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to the Prosecution bar. You see a somewhat depleted Defence bench. I should explain that for our CaseMap manager, he is in New York sitting his bar exams which we wish him the best of luck with. As for my lead counsel, Ms. Vidovic, she does have some health issues which hopefully will be of short duration. But it's a matter which perhaps we can discuss on Wednesday in any event, and see the situation. Perhaps I failed to introduce myself. I'm John Jones, co-counsel, and I'm joined by Ms. Jasmina Cosic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones, and good afternoon to you and your team -- your depleted team. Are there any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Usher, perhaps you could fetch the witness, please. The reason we are waiting is I was informed beforehand that the witness has been put in a room which is a little more distant than usual. So Madam Usher has to take her time to bring him over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am assuming that you are receiving interpretation like before. At any time there are problems with the interpretation, please draw our attention straight away. Second thing is: May I please remind you that you are testifying under oath. Last week you made a solemn declaration to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and that solemn declaration still stands. There's no need for you to repeat it every time you are taking that seat over there. Mr. Jones is -- will be proceeding with his cross-examination and then we'll see whether there is re-examination and there will be some questions from the Bench as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take your time. There's no hurry, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Mujkanovic, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You provided us a vast amount of information last week on a number of themes so I'm just going to tie up a few matters today. So we shouldn't be very long. Now, we speak at length last week about torbari and the social phenomenon about the torbari. We also came across the hapsi. Now, what do you understand about that term, hapsi?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that term. The phrase I'm familiar with is "catch him alive," because that's what the torbari used to say. It was some sort of a battle cry on their way into a village, probably meant to intimidate those still around in the village. That's what they would say on their way in: "Get him alive," "Catch him alive." The term refers to more or less the same thing, get him or catch him alive. It boils down to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if the Witness could be shown a copy of D199 which is a copy of "War Hospital." And I'm going to refer to two sections from that book, page 101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, Mr. Jones, "hapsi" is an Arabic word which has various connotations, one of which is a thief, the other of which is a person who has been in jail, has been imprisoned; in fact one other word which derives from "haps," which means prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fascinating, Your Honour. It may be also that I mispronounced the word. "Hapsi", I think, is the correct pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, it's page 101 and it's the seventh paragraph. It starts a little below the middle of the page. I'd read the section: "Sometimes Nedret travels to the field to meet people in the outlying areas. As a proud and curious member of the Srebrenica war council, eager to give confidence to the soldiers, he tours every yard of the front lines and visits distant medical stations. "He even witnesses some war actions, viewing the fighting from a distance and watching as thousands upon thousands of civilians pour in, like a lava flow, to pillage Serb villages. By their sheer numbers and the thunder of their voices, the howling, bag-carrying hordes help scare Serb inhabitants away. The rushing plunders have earned a fake military designation, the 'HPO division.' The H stands for 'Hapsi,' a Bosnian word for petty thieves. If 1,000 soldiers take part in an action, the HPO division adds at least 3,000." Just pausing there and I'll wait for the interpretation to catch up. Firstly, was it in Bjelovac that you saw this or was it elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in reference to the action against Voljevica, Bjelovac, and Loznicka Rijeka. As I said in the course of my testimony, I was with Ramiz Becirevic in the afternoon hours of the first day of fighting. I went to an elevation. It was quite far, though, 2 or 3 kilometres, and it was from an elevation from a hilltop that we watched this flood of people pouring into the villages. And that is what this chapter refers to, that particular action.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And seeing that expression there "hapsi," is it right that that refers to just ordinary people, civilian men, women, children, old people, civilians in short?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said it right at the outset. Those people, the torbari, are groups of people whose main objective was to snatch food, or rather items that they would later trade for food. They had these battle cries. Hapsi is not one of the ones that I heard at the time. They would yell things like "Catch them alive." It was a psychological aspect to the whole situation. It was meant to drive the remaining people out of the villages, leaving their houses and material goods behind so that they would be free to pillage and take whatever they could away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think you also said that they banged pots and pans also to make a great noise to make the people go away. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used all sorts of things to intimidate their opponents. There were battle cries and people were yelling "Allahu Akbar," Allah is great. They used all sorts of methods to intimidate the other side, to cause panic to arise and to make it as simple as possible for themselves to obtain their objective, which was to get food, food which was necessary for their survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then carrying on on that page -- you don't need to refer to it, I can read it. "It is the rumbling of their empty stomachs that sets these 'hapsi' on the heels of the soldiers. They come out of hunger and need and anger, many of them displaced from their own homes. Nedret sees them raging out of control, disobeying directives not to destroy things." So I want to ask you about that, "disobeying directives not to destroy things." Is it right then that in Bjelovac you were aware or saw or heard directives being issued not to destroy things but those directives being ignored by the civilians?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I can be a reliable witness for the Bjelovac action; I can only speak about what I saw at the time. And what I saw was a flood of civilians advancing on those villages. The author of this book probably got things mixed up a little, too. I would like to go back to what happened in Podravanje, as I was touring the area. And I saw a large group of people next to an excavator that was parked there. I started talking to those people. I had seen a haystack the haystack set alight previously and I told them, Don't burn this; just take whatever you need. And they replied: It's not us who are burning things, it's those other people. Nevertheless in this same spot where I met the group of people, a while later I saw the excavator catch fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I'll be asking about the torbari. Now just another question or two to wrap things up on the public health situation --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, if I may be allowed to clarify for the Trial Chamber. It may be a mistranslation or it may be a concept that is difficult to understand. Hapci is not the same as "hapsi." "Hapci" refers to thieves, people who steal things. It's a slang term, a colloquialism in the Bosnian language. So hapci would mean roughly speaking petty thieves, people stealing small and unimportant things, other people's chickens, bags of flour, that sort of thing. Petty theft. When you say hapci this is certainly not a reference to organised crime or bank robbers. Hapci may as well be a reference to a pickpocket. It's a slang term, really, a colloquialism. I don't think you're likely to find this term in any of the dictionaries that are available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When we see them referred to as the HPO division, the Hapsi division, that was a joke, was it? They certainly weren't a division of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, turning as I say to the situation in Srebrenica. In addition to all the problems you've described, there was no electricity supply in Srebrenica the whole time you were there, was there?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So what did you do in the hospital, in the operating theatre, to have light to operate by? Can you explain that for us.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the tallest odds we were facing, because the wounded were pouring in during both night and day. We always had to be prepared to receive them and to help them. There is a factory manufacturing industrial generators nearby. Those were used as sources of light, naturally. So for the first two and a half or three months, we used those generators. And once one of those was used up, we would trade the one that had been used up for a new one. There was another power generator that used oil, but we could only keep it working for a very short time because we were short of oil, too; there was no oil. We built a small water plant, in a manner of speaking, behind the post office about a hundred metres from the hospital at the small streak or creek that crosses Srebrenica. And this water plant produced as many as 2 and a half or 3 kilowatts of electric power which we used to have a light-bulb in the operating theatre. And we used the power also to operate the steriliser. This was how we extemporised. Sometimes this broke down, too, and we would use candles torch lights to provide lights to work under. It was all a large improvisation and nothing was as it should by rights have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it true that throughout Srebrenica there were people using improvised energy sources, for example using a bicycle to try and generate a radio? That sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we touched briefly on the issue of gangrene last week. Now, based on your conversations with Srebrenica fighters, can you say that it affected their morale to know that if they stepped on a mine or if they were injured they would have to be rushed to a hospital or operated on pretty quickly to stop gangrene?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that the fighters saw the hospital as a light at the end of the tunnel in the whole situation. The hospital provided extra security for them, a sense of security in combat. Most of them would say, If I'm ever wounded, if only I can make it to the hospital, I'm sure I will survive. Unfortunately it wasn't always like that. Sometimes vital organs would be destroyed or injured and they died on the way to hospital or on their arrival there. But our hospital certainly was a source of confidence and additional strength. They certainly did see it as a place of salvation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you aware, then, from these conversations that soldiers had to pull out of areas where there had been action pretty quickly because they had to get their wounded back to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The evacuation was a very difficult job. Usually a lorry with no top or cover was used to access these parts that could be accessed. And there was another van that we used. It had been used before the war by a bakery for bread supplies. Those were the two vehicles used to bring in the wounded. In order to get to this area that could still be accessed, even carts were used, carts drawn by oxen. It was very difficult to get the wounded over to the posts where they could be helped or back to Srebrenica for that matter. The distance to be crossed would sometimes be as much as 20 or 30 kilometres in order to get to the hospital and these evacuations took as long as two or three hours. This was an insurmountable problem and many of the soldiers were lost en route, during their transport to the hospital. But if you look at the lie of the land around and in Srebrenica, that's what makes it even more difficult to evacuate the wounded. It's mountainous terrain with steep rock-face and hills. Sometimes it would take as many as seven or eight soldiers to get a single soldier who was wounded evacuated and brought over to the nearest medical post.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because they're carrying him on their backs?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did whatever they could. Sometimes they had makeshift stretchers. Sometimes they carried people on their backs. They did whatever they could. We didn't really have a proper stretcher, the kind that should be used by any medical corps in the world. Sometimes the wounded are tricky to handle and you have to be careful about how you carry them. But those who evacuated the wounded did whatever they thought was best at the time with little if any expertise, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Moving to a different area, and apologies if I seem to be skipping about. But I'd like you to look at a photograph and caption from the book. And it's -- if you go to page 208 firstly and then basically three pages in. It's the page with the photograph of yourself at the top. It's actually the bottom photograph which I would like you to look at. And the caption there reads: "Because of a severe paper shortage, doctors wrote prescriptions on old medical records and other scraps of paper that could be found around the hospital." So my question firstly: Isn't that right that there was a paper shortage in the hospital and in Srebrenica generally, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. We couldn't even have proper medical files because there was no paper. If you wanted paper, it was something that you had to organise a search in order to get. People used it to roll cigarettes and most of the paper was used up that way, people smoking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you told us about seeing Naser Oric's signature or what looked like it on paper, was it on scraps of paper like these, like those that are shown in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, those were small shreds, slips of paper like the one you see here. A quarter, roughly speaking, of an A4-sized sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, last week you were shown a lot of documents which were typed on a A4 piece of paper. In the time you were in Srebrenica, did you see any typed documents of that nature?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, while I was in Srebrenica, I didn't see a single piece of paper like this. I was not even aware of any documents or orders that existed. Therefore, documents or papers are not something I can testify about. It was as late as a year ago that I first laid eyes on these when they were first shown me. I didn't even realise that someone was actually exchanging letters and documents at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. It may be an obvious question, but is it right that for you personally and the other doctors that you know that you weren't typing up notes about your patients with a typewriter?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is all written by hand. When patients came in, there was a book, a register, that we used where their first and last names, dates of birth would written down; this applies to everyone who was received at the hospital. And then the patients would be transferred to their respective wards, to their beds. There was a temperature list, a diagram, where their daily temperatures would be marked from the day they came in to the day they were discharged. Once the patients were discharged there would be some sort of a discharge letter written, stating what the treatment consisted of and what the condition of the patient was at his discharge, whether it was necessary to carry out any further regular checks at home, whether the patient should return to the hospital, or was entirely cured.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And those discharge letters were written by hand, if I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discharge letters were most often written by hand. While I was in the hotel, I slept there at the hotel and there was a typewriter at that hotel. So some discharge letters were typewritten, but a small number, 100 or 200 at the most. So whenever I had free time I wanted to organise this medical documentation and I used this typewriter. This typewriter was usually brought to my hotel room and I would type up discharge letters on the typewriter and I type it with my physician's stamp and sign them. However, the vast majority, 90 per cent of discharge letters were written by hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's the Hotel Domavija I take it that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Hotel Domavija.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you the only one of the doctors from the hospital who stayed in the Hotel Domavija? If you could answer verbally.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Pilav wasn't staying there?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He lived in Srebrenica with his mother and brother and somebody else. He was a refugee; he was not originally from Srebrenica. He had come there from the south-east area which had been occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Dr. Advo Hasanovic didn't live in the Hotel Domavija?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he lived in his apartment, which was some 2 to 300 metres from the war hospital in the direction of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, during your time in Srebrenica I think it's right to say that you treated between 35 and 40 patients of Serb ethnicity. Is that correct, firstly?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, yes. I couldn't give you the exact figure, but approximately that's right, about 40 people at the most. At the most, 40 Serb patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that you didn't see any signs of mistreatment on any of them?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I stated that already last week, namely that all of them were brought to the hospital as casualties, as people who were wounded. So they did not have any other injuries except for injuries inflicted by various weapons or various types of ammunition, be it shells or grenades or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And didn't you also treat Naser Oric for a leg injury shortly before internationals arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naser Oric is somebody whom I treated twice. The first time I treated him was shortly after my arrival in Srebrenica sometime in August. He had a wound in the area of the upper right leg; there was a shrapnel wound. And it had been inflicted some two or three months prior to my arrival, so it was a wound on his thigh. We performed surgery to take the shrapnel out. The second time I treated him was in April of 1993 when he was wounded on the lower left or right leg. I couldn't tell you now. But he had a wound -- it was again a shrapnel wound, a heavy -- serious wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And after that wound was he on crutches? Was he limping? Can you give us some idea of the extent of the injury.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was some 10 to 15 days before I left Srebrenica. On the day I left Srebrenica, which was the 22nd of April, Naser was in bed. I came to see him. We said goodbye. At the time he was still unable to walk, to move about. He was bedridden. After that I didn't see him so I couldn't really tell you whether he was able to walk independently or had some crutches or was limping. When I saw him, he was still in bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know when he sustained that injury, roughly?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to give you some rough idea. It could have been between the 10th or perhaps between the 5th and the 10th of April of 1993, around that time if my memory serves me right. Around the 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, again moving to a different subject. I have a couple of clarifying questions about the concept of the subregion which you spoke about being considered in late 1992 and early 1993. And with the usher's assistance I would like to pass up a new exhibit. The ERN is 03721404. Now, it's dated 21st of January, 1993, and it purports to be signed by Hamid Salihovic as president of the subregional War Presidency. Now, I won't go into the content of this document, but firstly, I think you told us the subregion never properly came into operation; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. But I have a different kind of document in front of me -- no, no, it seems that it is right. Yes, the signature is on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So is it right there wasn't ever any unified command for the enclaves of Kamenica, Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. There never was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you aware that Hamid Salihovic was working on the concept in January 1993, indeed in late January 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already stated that this idea of a subregion, the concept of subregion and uniting the enclaves in the Drina region appeared in late 1992/early 1993. The purpose of that concept was to pull together all human resources and material and technical resources in that area. I am not aware that Hamid Salihovic was the president of this subregion. I don't know what this man did. I only occasional saw him in the street, and I don't know whether he actually did something about it. Maybe he even did, but it didn't last long because very soon thereafter Konjevic Polje fell as did Cerska. So the whole concept lost practical Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. significance. And I couldn't really tell you whether Hamid Salihovic managed to put this into reality or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask that that document be given an exhibit number, Defence exhibit number. I think it's probably D 201.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's D202.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered and admitted in evidence and marked as Defence Exhibit D202.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. If the witness could now be shown P255, which is 01839515 to 0183 to 9516. And this is going to be the resignation document signed by Hamid Salihovic, Ramiz Becirevic and others which you saw last week. It's just on its way. Your Honour, if I may, as a preliminary we have a corrected version of the translation and it concerns the expression in the paragraph 3, third sentence, which I'll read first of all in Bosnian as well as I can which is "Mi nemamo ovlastenja ni mogucnosti da to razrjesimo nacelnik i komandant nepokazuje interes za to." That's been translated in English as "We have no powers or opportunity to dismiss the chief and the commander shows no interest in doing so." We submit that's not the correct translation. In our version it reads: "We have no powers or opportunities to do this and the chief and the commander shows no interest in doing so." We would like to submit our translation as a defence exhibit. We could also consider asking the interpreters which version they would prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean which -- the interpreters -- I don't follow you. What do you mean by asking the interpreters which version they would prefer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we're going to tender our translation as a Defence exhibit, but if it would assist the Chamber we could ask the booth to look at that sentence and provide an interpretation ad hoc or we can see with the translation section. Whatever course Your Honour would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: To assist the Trial Chamber and my learned friend, we can also ask CLSS by do an official translation in that respect with a view to the comments of my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. It needn't detain us, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so. If the Chamber has -- will encounter difficulties in this regard, if this is at all important, we'll find a solution ourselves. In the meantime this is going to be tendered as a Defence exhibit, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is D203. Which is the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, the third sentence. In English: "We have no powers or opportunity to resolve this." That's the difference, that one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkanovic, just looking at that third paragraph, that concerns the problem of vehicles, doesn't it, which I think you explained was raised by these people? I'm sorry, you have to give a verbal answer.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This involves a vehicle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were shown a Prosecution Exhibit P200 last week, which was dated 16th of April, 1993, which suggested that despite the letter of resignation in December, Hamid Salihovic continued in his functions until 16 April 1993. So I have a couple of questions about that now. Now, first, isn't it right that you didn't attend any meetings of the operation staff after 22 December 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended the meetings of the operations staff very rarely. I attended very few of them, two or three perhaps, for a very simple reason: because at the time while the operations staff was in session, I always had wounded patients in the surgery room and I believed that that had priority over attending meetings. So most of these things that I saw I saw for the first time in these documents; therefore, I cannot really tell you more about how these documents were drafted or what else was discussed at the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So it correct then that you don't know whether Hamid Salihovic attended meetings of the operations staff after 22 December 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I cannot claim either way, that he was present or not present. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So when you said that Hamid Salihovic continued working in his functions although -- despite the resignation letter, is that something which you recollect? Is that something which you can affirm, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is more likely that I don't know. I would see this man in the street carrying a small bag and looking like a person who is involved in something, going places, and so on. But I can't tell you whether he attended meetings or not. I don't know that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you say that his role in the operations staff as head of the department for security and intelligence is something completely different from being president of the subregional War Presidency? In other words, it was a different post all together; there was no continuity between the two.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not linked, no, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as far as the reasons which are set out in this letter for the persons resigning are concerned, is it right the persons here are complaining about the War Presidency primarily and that they're not receiving proper instructions about their competencies?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I can tell you -- only something about my contacts with them, but these were not formal contacts. There were no meetings there. I remember that there was always a problem with a vehicle, that it was always mentioned and discussed. We needed a vehicle at the hospital as well, but there was simply no vehicle whatsoever. Or if there was a vehicle, then there was no fuel. So in the end it all came to the same: Either you had a vehicle but no fuel or vice versa. But this doesn't deal with only vehicle but also with fuel, with the gas that was needed. So that was a problem that we had. It was a very urgent problem and I think that they appealed to the War Presidency to do something and to ensure that this vehicle was placed at the disposal of the operational staff and other people who signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to put a couple of propositions to you regarding this document and these resignations and tell me whether you agree that they're correct or consistent. In the opening speech made by the Prosecution in this trial on the 6th of October, 2004, Mr. Wubben made the following declaration about these resignations, and it's page 226 of the transcript: "Muslim military staff loyal and proud to have been led by Naser Oric felt forced to resign from the military staff post because of the increasing lawlessness in Srebrenica and because Naser Oric did not diligently exercise responsible command in time of war." Now, firstly, do you understand or did you understand that the reasons or one of the reasons for these resignations was because Naser Oric did not diligently exercise responsible command in time of war?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you one thing. First of all, I didn't know that there was any staff, a staff that existed before the operational staff. As I told you, I knew that there were local commanders in charge of units who would occasionally meet and discuss certain problems. I am convinced to this day that even if something existed on paper, a staff or something like that, that I'm sure that it didn't function in practice, otherwise there would have been no need for the operational staff. Another thing is that the commanders, local commanders, saw Naser Oric as their commander, as commander of that area in Srebrenica. All of them did except for one man, Hakim Eric. Therefore, I don't think that I could tell you whether people who signed this accepted Naser as the Srebrenica commander or not. All I know is that they did these things and Ramiz Becirevic in February was appointed chief of staff instead of Osmanovic, which means he saw him as his commander as well. So I couldn't really answer our question to the full extent, but I hope this answer I gave you is of some significance as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: First perhaps just one correction for the record: I think you said Hakija Meholjic again, didn't you, rather than Hakim Eric which is what we have.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hakija Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And secondly, when you talk about the area of Srebrenica, well obviously that excludes Bratunac. But equally, are you talking about the town of Srebrenica or a broader area?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "Srebrenica" I mean the territory of Srebrenica municipality which roughly corresponded to the area of sometime municipality of Srebrenica, including the people from Bratunac, Vlasenica, Han Pijesak, Zvornik, who lived in Srebrenica. I exclude Konjevic Polje from this concept of Srebrenica municipality in 1991 just before the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina started. Konjevic Polje represented Bratunac municipality, in fact, because it used to belong to that local commune. So I'm excluding from this concept Konjevic Polje which in my mind represents Bratunac municipality. I hope I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's clear. But when you talk about local commanders in Srebrenica, leaving aside the names and places which we've seen in documents, are you also including commanders let's say from Mocevici or Poznanovici or these other places that do not appear in the documents you've been shown?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand whether commanders from Poznanovici and Mocevici. I'm not sure which commanders you're referring to. Could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Do you exclude the possibility that there were commanders, let's say, in Mocevici or Poznanovici who didn't regard Naser Oric as their commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is leading to speculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No speculation at all. He either knows the answer or he doesn't. Of course he has been told in the course of the last week that we don't need speculation and we don't want speculation from him. So please answer the question if you are aware of what you're being asked by Mr. Jones. If you know the answer, give it. If you're not sure, if you need to speculate, then don't give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not sure -- or rather, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, finally on this resignation letter if we look at paragraph 2, and this is P255 still: "The OS staff has no official documents or instructions or from the BH OS Main Staff or War Presidency in wartime conditions. Work on such responsible duties assumes a great risk and vast opportunities to make large mistakes." My question is: If you're aware, is it not true that in December 1992 no instructions, laws or regulations had been received in Srebrenica from either Tuzla or Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By whom, first, and from whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: By the staff from the authorities in Sarajevo and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which staff? The operations staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. The OS staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. And who is Defence counsel referring to? That who receive received it in Srebrenica? All of Srebrenica or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Because the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The operations staff. And the witness -- if they did receive, the witness needs to tell us from who.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Operations staff. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you something that I know personally. I as chief of medical corps as a war surgeon received no instructions from Tuzla, Sarajevo, Srebrenica, or anywhere else as to what I needed to do. We were simply sent there and any good that we did was viewed positively and if we failed did something it was ignored. I received no official instructions or no formal regulation, qualifying whether what I had done was properly or not. Now, what I'm saying applies to myself personally, to somebody who was in charge of the medical corps. So whatever we thought ought to be done we did it. We didn't have any instructions, any formal protocols as to how things ought to be done. Nobody ever sent to us or gave to me personally any Official Gazette or any official instruction or regulation. Now, what I just said applies only to me personally. I can't tell you about others. But if we apply the same analogy, then it would be similar in case of the others. Nobody mentioned any laws to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And did you hear that when you personally attended meetings of the operations staff, complaints expressed by people that, We haven't received official decrees or laws or regulations?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from the War Presidency, from people who were involved in the operations staff. They would say that they lacked any legal regulations that would regulate their activities, and that's how it was. Nobody ever said to us that things ought to be organised in this way or in that way. What we tried to do was ensure that children were able to attend a school, that there were teachers. And it was very hard to do that. There were no regulations available to us. How can one organise school under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown P158 and the ERN is 01239545, and I'm going to be showing it just for illustrative purposes. I can provide my copy if it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I just want you to look at this document because as you'll see the heading refers to Article 18, paragraph 1, item 1 of the decree law on the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina as published in the Official Gazette. And I'm just wondering whether you found that strange in certain of these documents that they're prefaced with references to the Official Gazette, which as you told us as far as you were aware hadn't been received?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is dated April 1992. That was probably before the enclave was besieged or blocked in May. This is probably an Official Gazette where a state of war was declared. I really wouldn't like to speculate. I'm not sure what this is in reference to, but I can tell you for certain that I received no documents or instructions on how I was to organise the hospital. So this must be a copy of the Official Gazette of Bosnia and Herzegovina April 1992. It says 4/92. So probably this is something that was the case before the blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just have seven or so more documents to look at which were shown to you by the Prosecutor. P74, which is 02075809, and that's a purported decision dated 20 May 1992. Now, you were shown this document on Monday and you weren't able to confirm the signature which purports to be of Naser Oric. In fact there are two signatures, aren't there? There's also one on the left.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Hamdija Fejzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you see the passage towards the bottom, which states: "This decision is provisional and will be valid until the municipal, political and legislative bodies, Presidency and Assembly, are established. Bogilovic shall be temporarily accountable of his work to the Srebrenica TO staff, to the above bodies once they have been set up, and to the authorised institutions in Tuzla and Sarajevo when they too have been set up." My question is: Do you agree this is a provisional decision at best until the civil authorities are established?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say anything about this. I know that this person was indeed a chief of the public security station. So this must have been some sort of a provisional decision. I'm not familiar with the method of his appointment, so I can't comment on this. I can't tell you for sure wether it was provisional. But it must have been provisional because after the demilitarisation of the area was set up, Hakija Meholjic [Realtime transcript read in error: "Mehmedovic"] replaced him as chief of the public security station, which means that he had remained in this position until mid-1993 I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you aware that Becir Bogilovic was subsequently appointed to his position of chief of the public security station by the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Becir Bogilovic was a member of the War Presidency, though, wasn't he, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, the next --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the reason I don't know is that some people would come to meetings of the War Presidency on the strength of their position. On the one hand you had the members; on the other hand you had Becir Bogilovic as chief of the public security station attending meetings to answer questions concerning public order, that sort of thing. As to whether he was a member of the War Presidency or not, I really don't know. I know that he was always around somewhere. He dropped by the hospital every now and then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a matter of clarification. Line 25 under 5 there is a naming of Mehmedovic, Hakija Mehmedovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I heard him say "Meholjic." For the record, that stands corrected: Where on page 25, line 5, we have Mehmedovic it should read Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, the next document I want you to look at is the so-called war diary. I think that comes in one whole exhibit. The pages which I'm going to refer to now is 02115054 in the Bosnian. And in English that's 03090714. But firstly I just want to ask some general questions about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the P number, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The P --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 84, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And firstly, just general questions about this document. This document appears to be minutes of very meetings. In the meetings you attended, were these minutes ever adopted by the members as an accurate record of what had been discussed at the prior meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So these are just someone's notes of what went on?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest with you, I didn't realise that anyone was taking notes in the first place. There must have been someone taking minutes of what people said, but at the time I was not aware of anyone doing that. No minutes were adopted at the time; that's for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could please look at 02115054 and it's the minutes of the meeting of the Srebrenica armed forces operation staff held on 14 October 1992 at 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's page 10 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd just like you to look at the line which says: "Ramiz's proposal was put to the vote and was adopted unanimously." I don't know if you see that. It's the second paragraph on 5054 and you see Ramiz's name there. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, isn't that right that the way that the staff took decisions was actually by voting, voting on people's proposals?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, by voting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you're aware, wasn't that also the system for reaching decisions in the War Presidency, namely a democratic one where people voted on proposals?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Voting, yes, by voting. Majority votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So each person had one vote?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've explained the situation in the field as you understood it of how local commanders were chosen from the bottom up, if you like, rather than being appointed from the top down. Do you agree that that was also a democratic procedure in the sense that it was up to the people to choose who their commanders were?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely what I said. People who were commanders of those units were chosen or voted by the inhabitants of their respective villages. Usually the person selected would be the bravest man enjoying the greatest authority or reputation as a fighter in that particular village. It was not a matter of general authority; it was more a matter of choosing someone who displayed particular bravery in the first months of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Turning back to the war diary, that's pages 5042 to 5043. That's 02115042. In this case it's a meeting at which you were present in mid-September 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if we look at what's written on the second line it says, number 1: "The meeting was called to order by Chief O. Osmanovic who briefed those persons present on the tasks and departments. Nedret, Hamed A, Hamed S., Adil, Ramiz and Mustafa took part in the discussion. Our main task is to secure the unity of the armed forces." So firstly, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And so that's Osman Osmanovic, the chief of staff of the Srebrenica operations staff opening the meeting. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you recall him calling for military unity? In other words -- well, firstly, if you could answer that.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't specifically recall whether he did at this meeting, but I know that military unity was a conditio sine qua non: With no military unity, we would not have been in a position to achieve anything. It wasn't just a matter of one or two units, the overall structure has to display a degree military unity. My task was to talk to Hakija Fejzic to convince him to accept this concept of bringing military unity of the overall army structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We seem to have a bit of a curse when it comes to Hakijas. The last name, were you trying to convince Hakija Meholjic or Hamdija Fejzic?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would you agree that at that time, September 1992, there was not military unity in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said at the beginning of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to turn to a passage again in "War Hospital" in page 102 in which you're mentioned. It's the second paragraph in that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, at least as I read it in the transcript it seems to be an incomplete answer that we have. Your question was: "So would you agree at that time [Realtime transcript read in error: "point"], September 1992, there was not or there was no military unity in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the armed forces?" And the answer that we have is: "As I said at the beginning of my testimony." And it stops there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he needs to conclude it. He may have concluded it in his own language and this may have been interpreted the way I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I understood him to be saying "That's what I said at the beginning of my testimony."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not what we have in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was disunity throughout the military units and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's page 102 of "War Hospital" and second paragraph: "Part of the reasons the Serbs guard" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Line 24 of page 28 you put a question there which does not show up in the transcript, Mr. Jones. I do remember question was, that's when you commented that again this Hakija thing that we have. But could you recall your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question was was it Hakija Memdzic [sic] or Hamdija Fejzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he answered --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So the quote is: "Part of the reasons the Serbs guard humanitarian access to Srebrenica so jealously is that it's one of the free areas of Bosnia" -- is that correct? Let me just check. Sorry: "One of the few areas of Bosnia where Muslims have fought back successfully, with such punishing and brutal effect. Nedret credits himself with some of this success, priding himself for having helped broker cooperation between some of Srebrenica's rival commanders, men who might have preferred to kill one another instead of killing Serb soldiers." Is that true that you helped broker cooperation between commanders?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can certainly say that I did my best to link people up so that misunderstandings between local commanders may be clarified. I made several efforts and tried to get people together to talk and clear up any confusion. I'm not sure how successful I was, but at least I got people to talk. The intention was certainly good. The idea was that since the area was under attack at least we should avoid confusion in interpersonal relationships. I needed to do this as a human being, not in my professional capacity. I wanted to put my authority, my personal authority, to good use. People were inclined to trust me. I was a doctor in the area, after all. I wanted to take advantage of this role that I had or whatever authority I enjoyed to get people to talk to one another and try to clear things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Is it right that there were serious rivalries among commanders at the time you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back to the war diary, as opposed to "War Hospital" for a moment, and it's on the same page we were looking at earlier 02015042 and it's on the thing we discussed earlier. You can see Osman saying "A request should be sent to Sarajevo to send us all the orders, decrees, instructions, et cetera, that have been issued at the outbreak of the war." I don't know if you see that.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's just on the same point again and I think you've answered it, but you were aware, were you not, that there were problems in getting those orders, decrees, and instructions from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly there were problems. I'm not aware of any decrees or orders actually arriving. I can't say we received any laws or instructions, at least not to my knowledge. But there may have been something that I was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then just finally on this. We see Ramiz there, next to his name: "Formed units to avoid disorganisation." And then on 02115043 we see: "Priority tasks, formation of units. This should be done depending on the number of men and not on the number of weapons. Weapons must be registered." Seeing that, does that confirm what you were saying last week that Srebrenica's fighters certainly at this date were not organised into proper units?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would it be right also generally to say that no matter what was set down on paper in terms of aspirations, that didn't always reflect the reality on the ground?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We also see communications discussed on 5042 just above the bit we saw with Osman. Hamed: "A request for the provision of VHF lines should be sent to the Tuzla district staff. We hope that the telephone lines will soon be established." Now, firstly would that be Hamed Alic speaking, the person in charge of communications?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Hamed Alic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you confirm that the operations staff didn't have telephone or VHF lines at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had nothing. That's why I'm laughing. They say "before normal lines of communication are set up with Tuzla," which never happened. But people were optimistic and they chose to believe that soon there would be normal phone lines between Srebrenica and Tuzla and ways to get in touch. That's what people chose to believe. This approach was far too idealistic and it proved to be an illusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if the witness would be shown P270 and also seems to be the same as 01801586. Just for the record, it also seems to be P109 and also seems to be the same as 01801587. I'll just say that for the record. Just a brief question on this document. It's dated 2 July 1992 and it refers to a meeting of the Crisis Staff of Srebrenica TO. You see that in the first line. Now, have you ever heard of a Crisis Staff existing at any time in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear at the outset that there was some sort of a Crisis Staff when Srebrenica was first attacked in April 1992, something to the effect that there was a Crisis Staff. I really know -- I really don't know who the members were. But I know that people referred to something, an institution or a body, called Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. You were asked a number of questions about this document on Tuesday. The fact is, isn't it, that you don't know whether or by -- whether this decision was taken and if it was taken by whom it was taken, do you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm not aware of this decision ever being taken, and this was before I arrived. So I hadn't seen this document until last year and I can't offer any comments as to whether a decision like this was ever adopted or indeed in this form. Last time I said that I can make observations about certain people here. Halilovic, for example; I later realised that he was chief of the military police. Hamed Alic worked in the post office across the way. He operated the radio device. Becir Halilovic was chief of the public security station and Jusuf Halilovic was the chief of the civilian protection staff or this other person called Avdic and Mirsad -- and Senahid Tabakovic I knew in a different capacity, as local commander in Skenderovici. And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] confirm that this document was received by anyone or indeed that it was --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One more document before the break, and that is P99. This is the ERN 00926395. And in fact I would also ask that the witness be shown P100 which is the same document, 02066400. Starting with P100, in fact. P100 on the ELMO, please. Now, I wonder if I need to clear up that document. If you can look at that Dr. Mujkanovic. If we can go to the top of the document where there's a signature.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We see a signature at the top there dated 23rd of May, 2001. I need to clarify with you, Dr. Mujkanovic, were you ever shown by the Prosecution when you were shown Naser Oric's signature documents that had a signature like that at the top and a date or a date, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Dealing with this document, do you agree -- well, it's a handwritten scrap of paper from some notebook, firstly. Could you accept that description?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't tell you anything about this or what it is. I have no idea. You mean the entire page that I can see here? Or are you only referring to the dates, 23rd of May, 2001, 1115 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just the page. I'm sorry. You've only seen this page. You haven't it as part of any notebook or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this page with the text?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we have on the ELMO right now, this seems to be something that was actually torn out from a notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about the meaning of the phrase "everyone for everyone" which appears here. Isn't it a fact that as far as you know from your time in Srebrenica that the Serbs never returned any captured Muslims alive?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry. Can you repeat your answer. Are you aware of Serbs ever returning live Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was there from the 5th of August, 1992, to the 23rd of April, 1993, I never met any such person nor did I hear that a single live Muslim was ever returned or exchanged and sent back to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One passage in "War Hospital" to look at and then I'll be moving to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honour's hands whether to deal with that or after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long would it take you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can deal with that now and then we'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you can look at page 162 of "War Hospital" please, Dr. Mujkanovic. First of all, do you remember an American, Major Dudley, who was a forward controller for the US air drops?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page number you said, 162, yes. Yes, I do remember Major Rex Dudley, if I remember his first and last name correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And he left in April of 1993. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when it was that he left. But he was there when air drops were carried out. My impression was that his role was to coordinate the fly-overs and air drops. But I don't remember seeing him around in April, which would mean that he left before I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the passage I want to read is page 162: "US Army Major Rex Dudley departs the same day," and that's reporting to the same day as the convey of evacuees, "and reports back to high ranking individuals. His conclusions about Srebrenica were clear. The Serbs want to achieve free reign over the whole of eastern Bosnia. The besieged Muslim enclave, straddling a key line of communication, stands right in their way. The Serbs desperately want to take it out and they have a proven modus operandi: Take no prisoners. If the Serbs are allowed to capture Srebrenica, Major Dudley warns, the result will be genocide." My question is: As far as you're aware from your time there, was it the Serb policy to take no prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question, whether it was the Serb policy to do what? Can you please repeat the question. I'm not sure I got it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The policy was not to take any prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's difficult for me to say whether there was a policy in place like that. I didn't quite understand the question. What I did understand I find very difficult to answer. Do you mean whether Serbs wanted to take prisoners or refused to take prisoners? Maybe if you could rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me just put it this way: You never received a live Muslim exchange in the hospital, did you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can take a break there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, just three more documents to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown P3, please, and that's 00926461.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were shown this document by the Prosecution and it's a purported document dated 18th October 1992. And again, it refers to a decree law at the top. And it refers to a decree law of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In fact, it's right, isn't it, that there was no state called Bosnia and Herzegovina until after the Dayton Peace Agreement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina did exist. It was defined by the Dayton Accords as the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I think that it existed prior to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: At this time it was known as the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you help us with this: Can you see who is being ordered according to this purported order, or who it's being sent to?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say who this was sent to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because it's not apparent on the face of the document, is it?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, would you agree from the wording that the reference to "constant communication by couriers" is aspirational? In other words, it's not saying that it's happened but it's hoping to establish such communication by 25 October 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the 25th of October, yes, something that should happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, upon quoting this document there is a rephrasing by the Defence counsel stating that there is a hope, there is an aspiration. Well, this document is clear in the language: There is an order. So the question should be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, point taken. Mr. Jones --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know I need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it's going to change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't think I need to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness himself said that it seems to be an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, communication by couriers, would you agree in a sense that's the most primitive sense of communication? It's simply people running back and forth with messages.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly is the most primitive means of communication among people. Yes, I agree, especially nowadays when technology is so advanced. It is right, it is the most primitive means of communication, to send somebody with a letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that it appears from this that even in mid-October 1992 lower and higher units were not even in constant communication with each other, even by courier?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to interrupt, but according to paragraph 2 of the document there is a redaction like "I ordered to establish in full." That means that is suggested that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no I'll stop you here. No. I'll stop you. Not -- that's not the kind of interruption that I can allow when the witness has not yet started giving his answer. Yes, Witness, please, I'll repeat to you the question that was put to you by Mr. Jones and then please answer it. "Would you agree that it appears from the text from this that even in mid-October 1992 lower and higher units were not even in constant communication with each other, even by courier?" Would you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't provide an answer to that, Mr. President. I couldn't say whether the units were in constant communication via couriers or not. What I can say is that that was the only means of communication at the time in Srebrenica, communication via couriers carrying messages, mail, and so on. Sometimes there wasn't even a written order; they would simply be given verbal instructions to the effect: Go and tell such-and-such person and this and that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I've finished with that document. If the witness could be shown P164 which is ERN 03705211. For the record, this is a version it appears of P263 which is 03557343, but this has writing on it in Dutch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is so, I will let Mr. Wubben interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If it's permitted, then I would like to read into the record what it says in Dutch, and it's not my interpretation. In the English translation the Dutch reads: "The leader of the enclave announces a mobilisation to prepare an attack on the Serbian settlements." This is at the bottom. And this document also has Ferid i Jemso in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we see it on the ELMO? What number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P164, I have it here. Now, I have -- the P164 I have, Mr. Jones and Mr. Wubben, is the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. There is an English translation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And what you're referring to as words in Dutch I suppose is the sort of postscript at the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And also at the top it says: "Order by Naser Oric, 12th December, 1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in this document there's a reference to Glogova. Do you agree that Glogova was a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the document also refers to a mobilisation in Cerska, Kamenica, and Konjevic Polje, again all Muslim areas. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then the document says: "Be prepared to take on the enemy attack." Now, would you understand that as being a reference to repelling attacks by the enemy, by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would you agree that this document speaks of repelling attacks and says nothing about the Serb settlements, as the Dutch caption suggests?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on item 3, I would conclude that. "Be prepared to take on the enemy attack," meaning be prepared for the Serb attack on this area, Mackovac, Sandici, Kamenica, Previla. I'm not sure what is the name of this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have at hand the English translation of this document, 164 in English, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have mine. I can pass up my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that the official one you have been given by --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we don't seem to have it. Do we have it, Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we don't even have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It does say unrevised. It says OTP/DVU at the bottom and then ET and an ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't seem to have it even in the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm happy to make copies available of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, what's your position on this? Because I've asked for -- first of all, my colleagues pointed out to me that we haven't got the English translation and I am -- which is not a surprise because that happens sometimes, our secretaries sometimes do happen to leave out one version or the other. But what I am being told by the registrar is that we don't even have it in the records. For P164, we have one in the B/C/S language and we don't have the English translation, which seems to me strange as the translation that Mr. Jones had in his hand seems to be an official Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have some minutes to sort this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, my understanding is that we have that translation from the Prosecutor but that it wasn't necessarily exhibited with the document; in other words, I think we matched them up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I see there is that it is unrevised. So even if it is still unrevised we would rather prefer to have an unrevised translation of this document rather than nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can provide a copy of that translation provided by Defence counsel within let's say a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, there's no hurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if it has been revised in the meantime, please provide -- forward the revised version. If it's not, we're happy with the unrevised version for the time being at least, probably even for the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We'll see to it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you will, Mr. Wubben. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you read the third paragraph from the document you have for the benefit -- for our own benefit and also for the benefit of the public, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It says: "Take all security measures and be on the," and then there's a question mark, Randici [sic], Mackovac, Kamenica, Previla line. Be prepared to take on the enemy attack."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact it looks like Sandici, the first place name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, finally P79 [Realtime transcript read in error: "P69"] which is ERN 0207514, a document dated September 1992 and signed by Osman Osmanovic. Now, regarding this document, and bearing in mind that it concerns the operation staff of which you remember, is it right that Osman Osmanovic in that document is appointing the name -- those named people to their positions in the operations staff, the operations staff of the armed forces of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
