utterances.text: And he's submitting the appointment to the War Presidency for verification, it says there, and then for approval by the republican authorities. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would the sequence hierarchically be chief of staff proposing to the War Presidency; War Presidency communicating to the republican authorities at the top for approval for the appointments?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For appointing members of the operations staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I see Mr. Wubben on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I really couldn't follow this P69 as referred to by my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not 69, 79.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, P79.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So from the beginning -- in the transcript line 44, 5, there's referring to 69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am looking -- I -- it's not my fault of course but I do apologise to everyone because I am checking the monitor now on computer monitor mode and what we have there is exhibit P179. The document that was being referred to by Mr. Jones, if I understood him well, is P79.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: P79. Apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is completely different. So I would suggest to Madam Usher to bring -- it's not your fault either, to bring that document back and -- because it's not the one we are supposed to show to the witness and we give him P79 which is a document that we have seen already during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I thought I said P79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you certainly did. In fact, I went for P79 in my, but I wasn't following on the monitor because I was looking for my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. One can only look at one place at one time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, for pointing out the discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So you've answered the request which I asked about the hierarchical sequence?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I believe you did. If Your Honours bear with me for a moment, I want to see if that was answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, if it was, I suggest you go through it again. It's a question of -- before we had the wrong document, now we have the right document and I think it's only fair and would be wiser to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, Your Honour. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So looking at this document, Dr. Mujkanovic, do you agree that it's Osman Osmanovic appointing people to their positions --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And we had -- I think there was the same objection coming from you when Mr. Wubben put the question. Because he asked the question if I remember well the same you are asking it. And you had -- you stood up at the time and said he's not appointing, he is recommending or suggesting --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies if that's the objection. He's submitting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. Is that the objection you had in mind of saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That he's submitting appointments, proposed appointments, to the War Presidency for confirmation and then for approval by the republican authorities?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that Naser Oric or the name Naser Oric or his title does not feature anywhere in that decision, either as a member of the operations staff or as someone whose approval is being sought?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Nor even as someone who is being consulted about these proposed appointments?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, witness already stated in court for your Judges that Osman Osmanovic had to report to Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That sounds to me very much a comment on the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a comment on the evidence. Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have got your answer, so I would ignore it and pass on to the next question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Although I do feel obliged to clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As far as this document is concerned, there is no mention anywhere of consultation or approval by Naser Oric anywhere, is there?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this document is concerned, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, just a few final questions and we're finished with the documents. In the Telering programme which we saw on the very first day of your cross-examination, you said the following: "I was with Naser the whole time while I stayed in Srebrenica; it means that I factually fought in war under his command. I think all the best about him as a person and as a commander." I just want to ask you about that: "I think all the best about him as a person and as a commander." When you said that, was that a true expression of your opinion of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've told us how Naser Oric used to visit the hospital to see how people, wounded Serbs and Muslims alike, were doing and whether he expressed concern about their injuries and whether they would be handicapped or whether they would recover, and you said he did that out of humanity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If it's possible for you to give an answer to this: What do you feel Naser Oric's attitude was towards you? Or how did he react towards you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to say how he felt about me. He would probably be the best person to ask that. He -- what I can say is that my cooperation with Naser Oric during the time I was in Srebrenica was very proper and that he had a lot of understanding for the difficulties that the hospital faced. What was most important for me was to ensure that the hospital ran as smoothly as possible under the circumstances. And he devoted a lot of time and energy to ensuring that the hospital had all the supplies, that the food and medicine reached the hospital. So in that respect, my contacts with Naser Oric were extremely positive and I have always since that time seen him as a very respectable person. I've already said over -- in the course of the past few days about the operations in which he participated or did not participate. I think I am the wrong person to ask that. I can't tell you whether he participated in certain operations or not because I myself did not participate in them. I was involved in treating patients and working at the hospital. But what I can tell you is that people in Srebrenica and the fighters there saw Naser as a true born commander. Many stories were circulated about him as a fighter. I'm not an eyewitness, so I can't tell you anything about his participation and involvement in certain operations because I wasn't involved. But based on the stories that circulated, he enjoyed a very high level of respect amongst the people, both as a commander and as a person who can reassure people and instil hope in them that the area would survive and that in the end eventually they would be able to go back to their homes. I can also tell you that in my presence whenever we met Naser never talked about himself, never said, I fought here or fought there. He tended to talk about other people and extol their qualities as fighters and so on. He would frequently mention Smajo Mandzic; Sabahudin, I can't remember his last name, called Mrki; Safet Omerovic, Muji Sabahudin, called Mrki; Safet Omerovic [as interpreted], called Mis; Nurija Memisevic, called Nurica [as interpreted]. So he tended to talk about his fighters, his people, people whom he trusted. I never heard him talk about himself, therefore I can't tell you whether he participated in certain operations or not. He was a very charismatic person in the area of Srebrenica. This is my opinion. I think that he was quite young and he was a very young person who carried tremendous burden. He was only 25 years old and had no prior military experience because he used to be a policeman before that. People used to sing songs about him, so he was immortalised in several songs that were played and performed. He was known as a very brave, very able fighter. This is what people said in Srebrenica. This is how people in Srebrenica saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you for that very full answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The interpreters might be on the wrong channel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When the Prosecution opened the case against Naser Oric last October, Mr. Wubben said that Naser Oric was a: "Warlord who was drunk with power." Is that how Naser Oric struck you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not. Drunk with power? There was no power to speak of in Srebrenica. What sort of power? To be anything in Srebrenica where you could hardly survive. It was a punishment rather than power. I was punished, too, but I had to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you know, wasn't Naser Oric's popularity you referred to also quite regional in the sense that he was popular in Potocari, where he was from, and in Srebrenica other commanders were just as popular like Hakija, or Akif, and Zulfo?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naser is a native of Potocari, and of course that was his base. That's where his family was, his relatives. Potocari is part of Srebrenica, after all; it's not external to Srebrenica. What I can say is that the entire population, including the refugees who were in Srebrenica at the time, trusted Naser Oric a great deal and later, too. But there are people who disputed that. Nothing is ever absolute. Certainly that there were both individuals and groups of people who believed that this was an exaggeration or not quite what it was made out to be. But this is only too human, if you see my point; it's normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that there was a Srebrenica elite, if you like, of more elder educated Srebrenicians like Hakija who never fully accepted Naser, accepted him as a commander?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the usual problem you have in the Balkans and especially in Bosnia. There is a division between those who come from a more rural background than a more urban background. Even if the town is very small people perceive themselves as better, as a godsend to others. They probably found it difficult to accept that someone from a rural background participated in all sorts of roles and positions. Even if we speak about civil authorities, there was a lot of bad blood, people who were from the urban settlements and people who were from one of the villages, they would refer to people who had a more rural background in a derogatory way as farmers. But the problem, Mr. Jones, is that your personal value, your worth, is assessed based on where you come from. If you come from a town or a city, you are automatically made out to be more valuable or as belonging to a different intellectual class as opposed to those who come from rural backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We looked at the extract from "War Hospital" where Major Dudley warned that if Srebrenica fell there would be genocide. My question is: You've told us that while you were in Srebrenica over 2.000 civilians were killed by shelling, air raids, et cetera. Do you agree that the 1995 genocide was just a continuation of what occurred when you were there but on a larger scale?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Mr. Wubben, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And prior to that I would like to tender translations of P164.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P64E -- 164E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 164E. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to address several issues, four issues in total I think up to three-quarters of an hour or an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take your time. This is an important witness, perhaps one of the most important we've had so far. I've told you beforehand that I'm not going to limit either the Prosecution or the Defence and we will need our own time to put questions to him in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, I will refer to the transcript of last Wednesday and Thursday and I will quote the parts referred to by me. First it is Wednesday, 16th of February, 2005, page 5.298, Your Honour. And I quote -- there is a question about destruction of Serb property. The question is: "Would the same apply for the destruction of Serb property?" And your answer was: "Your Honours, I've already explained that the things that happened with regard to the Serbian property, houses, furniture, food, this was mostly caused by the civilians who wanted to get hold of food and things and that that thought could be used in barter, that would eventually again end up with them getting food. And that was the biggest problem of the Srebrenica enclave. There was no mechanism, there was no instrument that could have prevented that from happening." I would like to quote also from the transcript your answers first page 5.268. A question by Judge Agius: "What was torbari mean?" And your answer is in part: "They would enter villages prior to or after an operation, looting food and taking food and foodstuffs away. That's what they did. And these are the civilians that I was talking about yesterday who would wait for the army to seize control of the village before storming the villages themselves." And then again page 5.269 as I quoted that on top in part. So those two parts I refer to in my quotation and my question will focus on those issues, those issues of various military actions, attacks or combat actions, during your time in Srebrenica. And I would like to ask you: Will you please answer my questions in that respect with a simple yes or no or that you don't know. First question: The military offensive action on Jezestica, 8th of August, 1992. Were you present during that attack? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present in Srebrenica, but I don't know about the attack, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Next question: And the military offensive action on Fakovici, 5th of October, 1992, were you present during that attack, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the war hospital in Srebrenica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So you were not present at that attack, during that attack?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The military offensive action on Bjelovac 14 up to 19 November 1992, were you present during that attack on Bjelovac, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that I was at an elevation with Ramiz Becirevic, but that is quite a distance from the attack, 3, 4, possibly 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Last question: The military offensive action in the Kravica area including Jezestica, 7th and 8th of January, 1993. Were you present during that attack?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Let me move to another issue, that's the issue about Kemo and let me refer to the transcript of last Thursday. I will quote it, Thursday, the 17th of February, page 5.250. There is a question line 16, and I quote: "Q. Now you were asked on Monday about Kemal Mehmedovic, nicknamed Kemal from Pale. Was he also nicknamed Kemo?" "A. Yes. "Q. You said he was a difficulty personality with a very bad temper. Is that correct? "A. Yes, that's correct."

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And I quote again --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, there is still no question put forth to you. I just start quoting. Please pay attention to that. Page 5.251, line 2, an answer, and I quote: "A. At the time I didn't know the man. It was shortly after my arrival in Srebrenica. I didn't know who he was or who many of the other people were in fact. I only got to know them later on." And then I will quote in part, Your Honours, page 5.253 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just for the record, at the time referred to, 8th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would take it so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I start quoting the question, line 2, the question is:" Right. Now, concerning Kemo, isn't it right that you became aware from the moment of your arrival in Srebrenica or soon after that there were a number of individuals like Kemo who were out of control? "A. That's correct." Further on, line 14: "Q. If Naser Oric tried to control Kemo, Kemo probably would have killed him? "A. Yes." In my following questions I will refer to Kemal Mehmedovic as Kemo. And my question is - and will you please answer my question in that respect with a simply yes or no or you don't know - so you only came to know Kemo after your arrival at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And when you came to know Kemo, did you ever associate with him?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said no, definitely, but the interpretation came yes. It should be no, and in fact we have the interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that you never saw Kemo communicate with Naser Oric therefore?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will move to the other issue, and again I will quote from the transcript on Wednesday and Thursday, starting with Wednesday, Your Honour, the 16th of February. Page 5.230, I quote -- it's line 2 on that page. You stated, Witness: "When I arrived in Srebrenica, Naser Oric was the commander of the defence of Srebrenica; that's how he introduced himself to me. That's how the people" -- excuse me. I will start again. "A. When I arrived in Srebrenica, Naser Oric was the commander of the defence of Srebrenica; that's how he introduced himself to me. That's how people referred to him." And of Thursday's transcript, Your Honours, page 5.292, and I quote from line 9. That's starting the answer in part, second sentence: "There were a lot of people who looked a little bit -- who looked a little like Naser, bearded people, that sort of styling. "Q. Referring to that were -- that that were Naser imitators, people who adopted his look?" Your answer: "A. Yes, that's true, very much so." I have questions for you. Will you please answer my question with a simple yes or no. Naser Oric introduced himself to you as a commander of the Srebrenica defence. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did anyone other than Naser Oric introduce himself to you as Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did anyone else introduce himself to you as commander of the Srebrenica defence?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will move to another issue. And let me refer to the transcript of last Friday -- sorry, last Wednesday, and I will quote again. Last Wednesday, page 5.197 from line 7 your answer, and I quote in part: "I said that the entire area of Srebrenica was an unorganised area. Nobody could look after these people in the way it could be expected. There were no conditions in place for any kind of normal life." And further line 22, I quote: "In my view in that short period of chaos which involved a large number of refugees and large number of people who had been transferred two or three times from their original places -- original place of residence, in that short period of time nobody could organise any way of normalcy that is linked with a normal geopolitical situation." That last part of the sentence was page 5.298, Your Honour. And in the following questions I will refer to the war hospital in Srebrenica during the time of your stay in that town, and again will Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you answer my question in that respect with a simple yes or no or that you don't know. During your stay at Srebrenica did the war hospital function as a centre for medical aid?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if that question lends itself to a yes or no answer, given the complexity of answers that this witness has given on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I could -- I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's -- the question is being put in a very particular context, and that is the context of hostilities, armed conflict at the time. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just think in fairness to this witness if he feels that a yes or no won't capture it, then he should not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you. The question refers specifically to a war hospital and the question is also whether that -- the war hospital he was running functioned as a centre for medical aid. I think in a way he has already given an explanation, but if you feel that you cannot answer it by just a yes or no and you would like to give us some information on that, you're free to do so, Dr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The war hospital in Srebrenica in terms of how it was organised was the top-level medical institution in the whole Podravanje area between Zepa and Kamenica. If you consider the conditions under which we worked, the number of doctors and paramedics working there, the equipment we had, there was no way it could have been a relevant medical institution. This only speaks about our situation at the time. But other side the war hospital there was no other institution that could look after patients. We had no communication to any other medical centre to begin with. A patient would come; if we could help him we helped him, if we couldn't help the patient, the patient would die. That was all the help that was available at the time between Zepa and Kamenica; that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Mujkanovic. And I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that satisfy your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was functioning on the central function for medical aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thought so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And Dr. Mujkanovic, you told the court last Monday that from 17 April 1992 to 17th April 1993 the war hospital in Srebrenica provided for over 3.600 wounded and injured persons, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said it provided for over 2.600 wounded. I'm only talking about the wounded. 2.600 is the correct figure. 1.600 of them were soldiers and about 1.000 civilians. That would be the breakdown roughly. When I say "civilians," I mean women, children, elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And also that the surgical outposts of the hospital functioned in the periphery of the war hospital?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were reception surgical outposts; that was what we called them, with paramedics manning them, male and female nurses. That would be the level.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And were you as a war surgeon at that time able to treat your patients on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my primary task; to deal with patients on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one stood in the way. It was my basic task, my reason for being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did you provide medical treatment together with a total staff of around 50?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did you provide that medical treatment in conjunction with medical doctors?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, whenever that was possible. If not, technicians and nurses would assist me during operations. The best thing was if there were two of those doctors together performing an operation, but that was rarely the case. Everything had to be improvised and that applied to operations, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And was that tasking of medical treatments provided between you and the other doctors?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were five other doctors at the war hospital except me. Dr. Alija Zanic worked in Vrnecka Rijeka, that's next to the Domavija Hotel. He was into conservative medicine which means he treated weak people, old men and women who required no surgery. Those were cases of diabetes, high blood pressure, heart problems, heart-related problems, diseases of that kind. It was an outpost of the war hospital that served the needs of patients like these.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did Dr. Avdo Hasanovic carry out the function of manager of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And you told the Court that the hospital is told ahead of time in order to prepare you and the staff to receive the wounded, the casualties, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the hospital received information practically one day before certain attacks. Sometimes we would receive that information on the day of an operation, in order to prepare and so on. However, as we were busy every day, we worked every day, sometimes that information wasn't really of great importance to us because casualties would come in regardless of the attacks or independent of the attacks. Sometimes civilians were hurt on minefields or there were shelling attacks, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did you also have regular contacts with Naser Oric to update him regarding the health of the wounded patients?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Naser Oric came to the hospital, inquired about the condition of the wounded. I did not inform anyone about the condition of the patients. I did not inform the War Presidency or anybody else. Whoever was interested would come in and inquire about certain patients. And we at the hospital did not write formal reports and send it to any body, any organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did hospital staff manage to evacuate 60 wounded per helicopters and some 6.000 by trucks somewhere around 19 or 20 April 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you have the wrong figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please tell what you know about an evacuation in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When having discussions with General Morillon about the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, one of the conditions was to evacuate the wounded from the war hospital in Srebrenica. There were two attempts to evacuate patients prior to the actual evacuation. On two occasions we tried to evacuate the patients via the UNPROFOR helicopters; however, we were prevented from doing that by the Serb forces who shelled the soccer field or the sport field before we were able to complete it. So the actual evacuation took place between the 18th and the 20th of April, 1993. The UNPROFOR helicopter on that occasion evacuated 651 male patients. I know this figure for a fact because we used to put marks on patients. So 651 wounded men fit for military service were evacuated by UN helicopters to the university hospital in Tuzla, and over 600 civilian patients, including women, children, and the elderly, were evacuated via the UN trucks through Srebrenica to Zvornik. So a total of 1300 patients were evacuated during those six days of that evacuation operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. So that was quite an operation?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Bosnia and Herzegovina that was the largest evacuation operation of the wounded. There was nothing larger than that prior or after that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, I put the number of 6.000, that should be 600. So I was mistaken at that time. I apologise for that, but Dr. Mujkanovic clarified that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Wubben. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, you gave extensive evidence regarding a situation of certain chaos at that time. Isn't it the case that there were at the hospital hardships in respect of shortages of bandage; medicine; electricity, as we learned today; and food?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't wish it upon anyone to be treated in that hospital, even if that was their last chance for survival, because that hospital lacked everything. Everything you mentioned lacked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And that the work at the hospital, this was under hard conditions?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the hospital was shelled several times. There was several direct hits. Occasionally it would happen that we would finish surgery, take the patient to the bed, and he would be hit there by a shell in bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And is it so that you did under these circumstances the best you could?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did everything we were able to do, both I and my colleagues. It is certain that we didn't provide to those people everything they needed, but it is also a fact that we didn't just let them die. We did everything we could under the circumstances to the best of our abilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And that the staff including you at least managed to achieve a functioning of the hospital, as testified by you in your response to my questions?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that the hospital functioned as it did, meaning that we as doctors did our best to provide the best treatment from the moment patients entered hospital until they left it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move to my last issue as far as I see now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a -- I will start with referring to the transcript of last Wednesday, and I will quote. Wednesday, page 5.299. That's the only quotation that we expect is the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: There is a question, Dr. Mujkanovic, at line 7 and I will start with referring to that question focused on contacts with Naser Oric and that he never encouraged these practices, never encouraged burning or looting. Your answer was, and I quote: "A. I've already confirmed that in my testimony. I said that not only did he not encourage, he saw it as a problem that was a constant subject of discussion at the War Presidency. Naser Oric's position was that there shouldn't be any fires set to the property, but no one, nobody, could prevent that." I have some questions for you. Will you please answer my questions with a simple yes or no or you don't know. So it is your testimony that Naser Oric was aware of this problem of burning and looting?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everybody was aware, everybody knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And that this problem occurred during every attack?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wasn't sure if that was the problem of burning occurred during every attack or Naser Oric knew that the problem occurred for every attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it really calls for an explanation. But, Mr. Wubben, I would suggest that you be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And that this problem of burning and looting occurred during every attack?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost every attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And do you recall your opinion as to why Naser Oric chose not to prevent or stop that from happening?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. He never expressed that opinion. If Mr. Wubben has a reference for when in his evidence this witness has expressed that opinion, I would be grateful if he could direct me to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, at the moment things being what they are, we will be visiting this matter ourselves later on, too. But Mr. Jones is correct. The witness has never really said -- your question was: "And do you recall your opinion as to why Naser Oric chose not to prevent that from happening?" I think that is premised on his affirmation that Naser Oric chose not to prevent this looting and burning from happening. He's never made that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I suggest you should do - if you want to, Mr. Wubben, because I will never interfere with your questions - is to ask the witness whether to his knowledge Naser Oric ever did anything on -- in regard to this looting or burning, and then you may proceed with other questions. But I don't think we can allow the question that you put earlier on. So you need to rephrase it or start from a different...

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, are you aware that Naser Oric did -- do anything about this problem of burning or looting? Did he take any steps?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any specific case where such steps were taken. But I also know that it was impossible to take any steps because one didn't know the identity of a person who set a house on fire or stole food or something like that. You have to put it in the context of the events in Srebrenica. It's hard to give a yes or no answer. In an area where people were in constant search for food, it was impossible. There was no mechanism, no way of preventing this or sanctioning it. If you disallow the people to go and search for food, then you have to provide the food to them yourself. I think that people did what they could in order to ensure their survival. Now, if you want me to tell you that I know of a case where somebody was punished and sentenced to a prison term because of what they did, I don't know of such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because he's given a very reasoned answer to part of the question. That explains very much what you've stated in regard to the constant looting or search for food. You did not, however, cover in your answer the burning and the destruction of property. I can understand that searching for food and looting everything that could have become useful either one way or another could be explained by the situation in Srebrenica at the time, where there was a shortage of everything. But destruction and burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President Your Honour, in those days we ourselves wondered why would somebody set a house on fire if they were able to loot the house and take out everything they wanted? However, people tended to believe that due to the fact that Srebrenica was overcrowded, overpopulated, that there were so many refugees - and I mentioned this in an answer given to Mr. Jones - that there was also a tension between rural and urban residents. People tended to believe that they would be relocated to Fakovici, Podravanje, and so on. And out of fear that they would be relocated to a place which was 20 to 30 kilometres from the city, where they would be exposed to Serb attacks, they set those houses on fire. Most likely that was the reason. They wanted to ensure that they would not be relocated elsewhere. This is at least an explanation that I find plausible and an explanation that seemed to dominate in discussions with people there. I cannot understand why would somebody set a house on fire. My own house was set on fire in Brcko; it was done by Serbs. But I myself never understood, why would somebody want to destroy in five minutes something that was built over the course of ten years that represented a life's work of somebody else. So that's what people did, they would go and set a house on fire, set somebody else's property on fire. This is a sociological phenomenon and I cannot explain it. All I can do is give you my own personal view of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were the Serbs doing the same thing, burning and destroying entire villages and houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why do you think they were doing this? Why do you think they were destroying villages and entire villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know I can answer that question. They probably also believed that by burning villages or houses they would deter the people from returning. In the Balkans, people are very attached to their houses, unlike the situation in the US or in western Europe where people do not pay too much attention to a house because that's something that can be easily changed. People in the Balkans can very attached to their house. They come to a place, build a house, regardless of whether they will have a job in that town, in that place. They build a house and become so attached to it that it becomes a part of their mentality. And this applies to people living from Greece up north. People get attached to an area, regardless of whether they have a job there or not. Here in Holland people do not build emotional ties to a certain geographic area; they will go and live wherever they can find a job. I don't think I'm a witness who can fully answer this because you really need a sociologist, a person who can explain this phenomenon of burning and setting houses on fire and looting them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I put it to you that that could also be a reason why Muslim civilians and soldiers, I don't know, burnt down and destroyed Serb houses and Serb villages so that the Serbs would not return to those villages. Would you accept that as one of the plausible reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I could accept that. This is one nation, Your Honour Mr. President, however people in that nation have three different religions; however, their feelings and philosophy are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you hear -- did you ever hear anyone explain the destruction of and burning of houses in this manner, that is to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I heard such explanations also in Srebrenica. People would say, Well, they burnt my house, too. If I don't set their house on fire, they will come back to the area. So that was one of the explanations given, yes. There were such cases. They wanted to ensure that people would not come back and live in the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben, but I wouldn't like to comment on whether the Dutch love their houses as much as the people in the Balkans or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will remain silent, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, now returning to the steps taken or not. To summarise, is it your testimony that you're not aware of any such steps taken to prevent this burning and looting?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that there were no cases where anyone was prosecuted for having set a house on fire or having looted a house. I can't say that no steps were taken to prevent that; however, there was no mechanism available to prevent people from doing that, from going to a village and burning houses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And does that include that you're not aware of any steps taken by Naser Oric to prevent that burning and looting?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He said there's no mechanism available, so I'm not sure what steps he should have taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, objection sustained. Perhaps you can rephrase your question, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Apart from the mechanism you described, are you aware of any steps taken by Naser Oric to prevent that burning and looting?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The mechanism he was saying -- no steps could be taken. So if you want to ask the witness what could be done to stop it and then were those the steps taken, that's one thing. But he's saying it was impossible. So what is Naser Oric supposed to have done?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben, you can ask the witness whether to his knowledge Naser Oric ever tried anything to curtail on this practice or tried to do anything, of course failed because there was no mechanism.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there anything to be done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's your witness, Mr. Wubben. I'm not going to put the question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The question is, Dr. Mujkanovic, whether to your knowledge Naser Oric ever tried anything to curtail on this practice or tried to do anything in respect to prevent this burning and looting.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've already stated that the villages were burned by civilians, people searching for food, in quest of food, and they would loot and take the food and then after several days, they would go and set houses on fire. It was not within the competencies of Naser Oric to monitor over what civilians were doing. If anybody should have done something, it should have been civilian protection or civilian authorities or the War Presidency; they should have done something. These villages are up to 30 kilometres from Srebrenica. Perhaps you don't have a realistic picture of that terrain. These are places very distant from each other. One is on a hill, the other one is elsewhere. So these villages are scattered over the area; they're not linked. There is no streets linking them. And they're called villages, but they're tiny. Some of them have five houses and the houses can be 1 kilometre away from each other. So these are not significant settlements. It was impossible to ensure safety there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And, Dr. Mujkanovic, are you aware of any reason why Naser Oric chose not to take any steps as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He didn't say that Naser Oric chose not to take steps. He's putting words in the witness's mouth and ignoring all answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, objection sustained. And this time I'm not telling you how to rephrase the question, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, are you aware of the reason why Naser Oric did not make any steps to prevent or stop this burning or looting?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's exactly the same question. It's already assuming that Naser Oric --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's not the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's not exactly the same, but it assumes that there were steps that he could take and that he didn't take them. The witness hasn't said that there were steps which could have been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness was not aware of it and he explained a reasoning and to his opinion Naser Oric had no competencies in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So he has answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: If that is the reason. So shall I put it in that way, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Mujkanovic, you have already explained that according to you Naser Oric did not have it within his competence and within his authority to try and curtail. Is that the only reason why he wouldn't have intervened in trying to curtail these burnings and destruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said this was one of the reasons: He was in no position to discuss this with civilians. But the most important reason, the paramount reason, was that there was simply no way to secure the areas. Those are enormous areas. I think you should go there and see for yourselves; maybe you would have a different idea then. It's a mountainous area with scattered villages. You would have needed 5.000 people to secure all those settlements from all those civilians that came hoarding [as interpreted] in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was just conferring with my two colleagues. How much more do you have, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I think it will take a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were going to suggest the following. I am not feeling that well. I think I'm running a temperature and I would rather go home the earliest possible. But what I was going to suggest is rather than have a break now and resume -- have you finish and then we start with our questions, that you finish with your questions as -- I mean, I'm not rushing you, but try to finish. We continue for the next 15 minutes and we finish for the day and we continue the next time, if that is acceptable to the interpreters and staff. All right. I see hands up. Is that acceptable to you, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And to you, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can we confer together were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: For one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Alternatively, Mr. Wubben, we could finish now and adjourn until Wednesday. You could finish on Wednesday. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. We would like to finish on -- yes, Your Honour, I appreciate that we would like to finish on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, because I would like to go home as quickly as I can because I'm not feeling -- I'm concentrating all right but it's getting worse as we go long. I don't want to end up in bed for the next three days or four days. We stand adjourned until Wednesday in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 23rd day of February, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.51 p.m.,
